From Deepground to Glenn, will the FF7 Remake finale manage to tie up all the series' loose ends?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Square Enix has given itself a monumental task with the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy. You would think simply retelling the story of the 1997 PS1 RPG classic with modern production values would be a tall order in itself, but this reimagining ambitiously pulls in elements from the metaseries that is Compilation of Final Fantasy 7 while also expanding it with multiple, even infinite, timelines.

In a GamesRadar+ interview, game director Naoki Hamaguchi told us, "The mission the team has is to basically recreate a new Final Fantasy 7 that includes all of that wider universe content from the start. So that's all consistently part of the world in the games that people will be playing."

With Final Fantasy 7 Revelation being the final part to this trilogy, and reportedly no DLC to follow, it's essentially the last chance to, as Hamaguchi puts it, "give the fans as much of the things that we know they want to see, the content that they want to look at, and we've included quite a lot of those references and connections to the wider Final Fantasy 7 universe in the last game."

It won't however just be a case of dolloping fan service for the sake of it, because if this finale is to truly stick the landing, it will also need to resolve the many new dangling narrative threads it has created in the previous instalments. Here's just 8 questions I have that I hope Final Fantasy 7 Revelation answers before I finally see credits on this epic reimagining. And of course, when you turn 8 on its side, it's also infinity!

Be warned, there will be some major spoilers covered here! And if you want to get caught up, we already have the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy story-so-far to help you out.

With the remake trilogy drawing to a close early 2027, we get ready for the epic conclusion with our Final Fantasy 7 Revelation Big Preview across hands-on impressions, dev access, and deep dives into the whole adventure so far.

The most devastating part of the original Final Fantasy 7, and worst kept spoiler, is Aerith's death. Its impact is all the more heartbreaking as she really is gone for good in your party. However, Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth's handling of the beloved flower girl's fate is more ambiguous, as even though a timeline distortion means Sephiroth does kill her and we see the party mourning her, Cloud still perceives her presence, though whether this is her ghost or perhaps an Aerith from an alternate timeline or an omnipresent form from the Lifestream is unclear.

But, even if I don't expect Aerith to be among your party members in Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, her prominent appearance in the game's key art should be enough evidence that she still has a significant role to play in this reimagining's story, whether in the current timeline or another.

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

While Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth explores a timeline where Zack survived the ending of Crisis Core, it largely amounts to him existing in an alternate timeline separate to what Cloud's party is doing until its mind-bending cross-universe final boss. But will he stay benched in Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, or is it possible that he could find a way to play a bigger role by crossing into the current timeline, much like Biggs (who crossed the other way)?

Either way, if Final Fantasy 7 Revelation continues following the original plot beats, then the truth behind Cloud's role in the events of Nibelheim will definitely involve Zack, though it's also possible that the Zack of this alternate timeline will also experience these events as a flashback through a different perspective when it comes to helping Cloud reconstruct his true memories.

Final Fantasy 7 Remake's Intermission DLC had thrown a curveball by introducing Shinra's top-secret military organization Deepground, having first appeared in PS2 spin-off Dirge of Cerberus as part of the Compilation of Final Fantasy 7.

Supersoldier Tsviet, Nero – Intermission's final boss – is undefeated, and Sonon ended up sacrificing himself so that Yuffie could escape, so there's a chance that we won't have seen the last of him, or indeed other Tsviet members. Tsviet leader Weiss, for instance, only makes a brief appearance, and his own boss fight is an optional one within the virtual reality training device.

The group are conspicuously absent throughout FF7 Rebirth. Perhaps they will come to the foreground during the section in Final Fantasy 7 Revelation that takes the party back to Midgar, maybe as a chance for Yuffie to get revenge and to show how far she's come.

The tensions between Shinra and Wutai have had more prominence in the remake, with the latter openly declaring war on the former towards the end of Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth. From our previous hands-on of Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, we know that the Wutai region itself will feature in the main story, whereas it had been completely optional in the original game (as was Yuffie, herself, as a party member).

The big question that remains is the driving force behind this conflict, which comes from former SOLDIER and Shinra defect Glenn Lodbrok, a character who incidentally first appeared in the now-defunct mobile battle royale spin-off Final Fantasy 7 The First Soldier, and who had already died at Rufus' hand. (A popular fan theory even persists that Lodbrok may actually be Cloud's father). While the end of Rebirth reveals that this version of Lodbrok was merely a black robe used by Sephiroth, it still leaves questions over his relationship with Wutai's interim Viceroy Sarruf, whose identity remains a mystery, and which our party may uncover while they are in the region.

Of the new characters introduced to Final Fantasy 7 Remake's universe, Roche might be one of the most intriguing. Essentially Final Fantasy's equivalent of Yakuza's Majima, he seems to just live for the thrill of taking on Cloud, who he considers his rival, despite being just a 3rd class SOLDIER. Yet his flamboyant motorcycling days were also tragically cut short when he volunteered to become a Sephiroth clone for Hojo, and ultimately became another lifeless black robe, encountered in the Temple of the Ancients. But, unlike the others, he still seems to hold onto some memories of his rivalry with Cloud.

Yet, if that was the end of Roche, it doesn't explain how he managed to survive the events at the end of Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth. He's the only one of the black robes retrieved from the temple by Hojo and Rufus, and taken back to Midgar. Could it be that there's a chance of redemption for this former SOLDIER to return to his former self in the same way Cloud does in the original story? Or does something worse await at the plated city?

With this finale the last chance to pull in other characters and references from the wider Compilation of Final Fantasy 7 universe, there's a likelihood that no character however minor isn't on the table for Final Fantasy 7 Revelation. While we've already speculated another return for Deepground, and it was already teased from the State of Play that former Turk Cissnei – vital to the plot of PSP prequel Crisis Core: Final Fantasy 7 – will be having a more proactive role in the main story following her appearance in Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth, there's the possibility that another character could make an 11th hour debut.

Given that there's already been more backstory to the black robes, and if more of Zack's story is explored, it would make sense to carry over the prequel's continuity, which may mean the appearance of its antagonist, Genesis. Sure, he may have been out of action by the events of the original story, only to re-emerge at the end of Dirge of Cerberus to little consequence like a botched Marvel Cinematic Universe post-credits scene. But, with different timelines, anything is possible, so perhaps this will now finally matter. After all, the original game was remade in 2022 as Crisis Core: Final Fantasy 7 Reunion, so it'd be weird if it didn't add to the remake saga's narrative proper.

Cid's appearance in Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth meant rejigging the original story's chronology of when the party meets him, but in Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, the pilot is a fully playable party member, which also means we should expect to uncover his backstory in Rocket Town.

Fans will however note that Cid's personality in Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth isn't quite the foul-mouthed chain-smoker that he was in the original game, though given he introduced himself to the party as the business owner of Bronco Airlines, you can probably reason that he needed a more courteous facade for his customers. The question is whether or not that mask will slip once we get to Rocket Town, and just how faithful the modern retelling will be to Cid's emotionally and mentally abusive treatment of Shera.

Sephiroth had been an elusive villain for much of the original Final Fantasy 7 until you finally faced him in the endgame. However, given he has been the final boss in both Final Fantasy 7 Remake and Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth, with each encounter more epic than the last, it presents a problem of just how on earth Final Fantasy 7 Revelation's final battle is going to play out without running out of steam.

It should be noted the game has yet to reveal Sephiroth's final, angelic 'safer' form, although the party has already faced his 'reborn' form (referred to as Bizarro in the original game) in Final Fantasy Rebirth, while a scene between Cloud and Sephiroth at the end of Final Fantasy 7 Remake was almost a shot-for-shot recreation of the very final cinematic fight at the end of the original game. Perhaps we'll see an all new ultimate form, and potentially another battle that transcends timelines, but I'm intrigued how the developers aim to top what has been done already while staying fresh. Whatever it is, I suspect you won't be able to win just by summoning Knights of the Round.

Our best Final Fantasy games ranking is a revelation when it comes to finding something new to play to plug the gap while you wait for more, while our best RPGs, best JRPGs, and best ARPGs lists have even more!

#4031. "Keep talking about it": Raw Power Games call for Wishlist aid as they, and their historical strategy sandbox Chronicles: Medieval, lose funding

Raw Power Games, an independent studio comprising veteran developers of The Witcher 3, Total War: Three Kingdoms, and Crusader Kings III (among others), have called on players for support after losing their funding - an existential threat to both the organisation and to their debut, the still-in-development historical strategy game Chronicles: Medieval.

In a statement posted last week, Raw Power announced that "the necessary funding" behind the studio was no longer in place, despite Chronicles: Medieval – which was unveiled last year with an expensive-looking, Tom Hardy-narrated trailer – apparently being within touching distance of its planned early access launch. Hardy or no Hardy, however, the statement declared that they aren't "going down without a fight", hinting at talks with what could be possible new investors, asking interested would-be fans to "keep talking about" the game, and encouraging its inclusion on Steam Wishlists.

A few days on, the impact of this rallying call remains unclear. Raw Power Games have made no further statements, and Chronicles: Medieval does not seem to appear on Steam's own list of Top Wishlisted games. SteamDB have it at #26 in their desire-o-rankings, representing no change from its position immediately before the funding announcement was made, and while the game's Steam follower count has increased by over 1,000 week-on-week – significantly more so than surrounding games in the list – that doesn't feel like the kind of wild grassroots support that might save a dozens-strong studio.

Still, as my childhood television used to say, every little helps, and I'm inclined to hope for Raw Power's survival if only as an antidote to the enthusiasm-poisining dread of seeing so many other developers being laid off and shut down. Chronicles: Medieval looks promisingly ambitious too, mashing up sprawling Mount & Blade-style battles with an RPG-flavoured strategy layer that involves the player's custom-created character ascending the snooty social hierarchy of 14th century England. Best of luck to everyone trying to get it over the early access line.

#4030. GTA 6 Launch Leads to Special Holiday for All Palworld Dev Employees

GTA 6 launches in one week's time, and the anticipation and excitement for the game is hard to ignore.

Rockstar Games' inbound open world action game is going to be a major cultural event when it launches on 19th November, and it seems some companies are recognising that — most notably, Pocketpair, the team behind Palworld.

The Japanese studio has announced that all employees are officially entitled to a period of leave from 19th to 23rd November so they can enjoy GTA 6 over an uninterrupted five days.

"On November 19, millions of gamers around the world will find themselves sitting at school or work, gazing longingly out the window, knowing that a new era of gaming is about to begin," the statement reads.

"At Pocketpair, we believe that such a historic occasion deserves our full attention. Therefore, after careful consideration, we have decided that all employees who intend to play Grand Theft Auto VI will be granted a special five-day holiday."

It's a move that's going down extremely well on social media, as you'd expect.

GTA 6 is reportedly causing a big spike in employees taking annual leave, with US employers estimated to lose a combined $1 billion of business on the 19th thanks to staff staying home to play.

Pocketpair isn't the only company offering time off; Logitech has announced Logi Game Day, an initiative that grants all employees a single day off for the purpose of playing video games.

While this can be used at any point over the next 12 months, the timing of its arrival suggests it's been implemented with GTA 6 in mind.

A while ago, a smaller business, Burger Motorsports, announced its intention to observe a day off for the game too.

It seems there are some businesses out there trying to get ahead of the curve. For what is almost certainly the biggest game of the decade, I think it's a smart move.

#4029. Three New Console Features Begin Rolling Out Today For Xbox Insiders (November 12)

Including a "Shuffle" feature for dynamic backgrounds!

The announcements are coming thick and fast today! This latest one is for Xbox Insiders, and it concerns three new console features that are rolling out now to members of the Alpha Skip-Ahead tier (with more tiers followed by a public release in the future).

Arguably the most notable one is the ability to rotate dynamic backgrounds - this means can turn on the "Shuffle" feature to display different backgrounds on a hourly, daily or weekly basis. You can also now organise your Xbox Disc to Digital titles more effectively, while there's even the ability to move the Xbox guide over to the right!

Let's take a look at all three features, and you can let us know what you think of them in the comments.

On this page: Three New Console Features Begin Rolling Out Today For Xbox Insiders (November 12)

To save a favorite, go to Settings > General > Personalization > My background > Dynamic backgrounds > Dynamic backgrounds, choose a background, and press X. You’ll find it in the new Favorites category. Pro tip: If you have a controller with an exclusive background, like the XBOX Wireless Controller X25 Special Edition, saving that background as a favorite lets you use it even when the controller isn’t connected!

You can also choose Shuffle at the start of any background category. Have your background change each time you sign in, or set it to change hourly, daily, or weekly. Shuffle your favorites or explore a whole category, it’s an easy way to keep Home feeling fresh.

Starting today, XBOX Insiders who’ve claimed a digital license from a disc-based games will see those games in a separate category in their full library. Prefer to keep them alongside your other owned games? You can switch back in Settings > General > Personalization > Games & apps. From that same page, you can also hide the digital license icon on game tiles.

Prefer the guide on the right? Now you can put it there. XBOX Insiders can choose whether the Guide opens on the left or right side of the screen to switch up how you navigate XBOX. Pick your side in Settings > General > Personalization > Guide. Tell us if you’re team left or team right.

The Primals' Eikichi Iwai has died at the age of 57.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Final Fantasy 14 players have been gathering en masse across servers today in the wake of the news that Eikichi Iwai—the bassist behind the game's band The Primals—has passed away at the age of 57.

A post went out on The Lodestone in the early hours of this morning (November 11) which read: "Thank you very much for your continued support of The Primals. As announced earlier today, we are deeply saddened to share the news of the sudden passing of bassist Eikichi Iwai.

"Having witnessed his truly unforgettable performance on stage at the recent Final Fantasy 14 Fan Festival in Japan, the sudden news of his passing has come as a profound shock. The members of The Primals and the entire FF14 Development and Operations teams are overcome with deep sorrow.

"As we reflect on all that Eikichi-san has left behind, our thoughts are with him, and we offer our heartfelt condolences."

The Primals is Final Fantasy 14's in-house band, fronted by composer Masayoshi Soken and localisation lead Michael-Christopher Koji Fox, and accompanied by Tetsuya Tachibana, GUNN, and Iwai himself.

Iwai's bass in particular has elevated a ton of already-excellent tracks across the game's history: Stormblood's Amatsu Kaze, Shadowbringers' To the Edge, Endwalker's Scream and Close in the Distance, and Dawntrail's Ride the Rhythm just to name a few. The Primals has just come off the back of a strong year for live performances, too—from their usual appearance at all three Fan Festivals that took place this year, to even taking the stage at the UK's biggest rock and music festival as part of Download's lineup.

A quick trip through some of Final Fantasy 14's European servers have seen tons of players gathering in main hubs like Limsa Lominsa to pay their respects and share what it is about Iwai's work that meant so much to them. As I write this story, players and campfires line the perimeter of Omega's Limsa Lominsa plaza—a common practice for honouring the passing of key community figures and beyond, something which I've previously witnessed for the likes of Berserk's creator Kentaro Miura and Dragon Ball creator Akira Toriyama.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

It's a small gesture, but one which is a pleasant reminder of why Final Fantasy 14 continues to maintain such an iron grip on myself and many others.

Mollie spent her early childhood deeply invested in games like Killer Instinct, Toontown and Audition Online, which continue to form the pillars of her personality today. She joined PC Gamer in 2020 as a news writer and now lends her expertise to write a wealth of features, guides and reviews with a dash of chaos. She can often be found causing mischief in Final Fantasy 14, using those experiences to write neat things about her favourite MMO. When she's not staring at her bunny girl she can be found sweating out rhythm games, pretending to be good at fighting games or spending far too much money at her local arcade.

#4027. Fate of the Galaxy is a huge, fully-featured Star Wars space combat sim that, thanks to being a total conversion mod for Freespace Open, even runs on my rubbish laptop

Star Wars has been back in the news recently because, to cut a long story short, the US alt-right have decided that Darth Vader was actually the good guy. We are not here to indulge such buffoonery. We are here to talk about Fate of the Galaxy, a free unofficial space combat simulator set during the events of the original Star Wars trilogy, featuring several mission-based campaigns and a stable of Imperial and Rebel Alliance ships that ranges from the quad-blasting X-Wing to Boba Fett's Firespray 31. Also, Naboo starfighters, if you really must.

It's a total conversion of poor dead Volition's venerable dogfighter FreeSpace 2, running on the open source Free Space 2 Open engine via the popular Knossos launcher. You don't need a copy of FreeSpace 2 to play it. You also don't need to pay. And nor do you need a whizbang PC – this bucket of bolts hums along happily on my i5-1145G7 with no dedicated graphics card. As the Rancor said to the padawan: finally, some good food.

Fate of the Galaxy has been in development off and on for almost two decades, weathering a number of team changes and shifts of focus. The FreeSpace Wiki has a longer account of its travels. It's not an officially licensed Star Wars production, as made evident by a scrolling text intro which takes the official orchestral theme and moves every note up or down a place, as though spitefully jolting the piano around under John Williams' fingers. It's not quite as bizarre as Portsmouth Sinfonia's Also sprach Zarathustra but it did make me cackle like the Emperor contemplating a freshly made asteroid field. But then I began playing, and my presumptuous merriment became a frown of concentration.

While hardly Steel Battalion, Fate of the Galaxy is a proper nerdy sim with a bustling 3D cockpit and all sorts of keyboard shortcuts to try once and immediately forget. You'll need to funnel energy between fore and aft shields during bombing runs on Star Destroyers, target individual subsystems with your ion cannon, give orders to other pilots, and consider whether to synch different guns for maximum effect. I can run the game fine on my work laptop with integrated graphics, but I'm definitely feeling the need for a beefier keyboard. And also a joystick. Certainly, I'm not going to get far in LAN multiplayer with this hunk of junk.

It seems a very generous production, based on 30 minutes playing kiss-chase with TIE bombers. The story campaigns and quickfix stand-alone skirmishes aside, there's a mission editor with text-based files for easier sharing. There's also VR support with head-tracking, should you own one of those haunted helmets. Learn more via the online manual (Google Doc), and find Fate of the Galaxy itself on Moddb. You'll need around seven gigs of disc space.

This being the year 2026, there's the question of generative AI usage - a topic of much concern lately in modding circles. Fate of the Galaxy's official site boasts that all the visual assets were "made by humans only". I'm less sure about other aspects – there's seemingly some artificial VO during the tutorial, though it sounds like antiquated, less insidious robocaller software. The FreeSpace Open engine itself greatly pre-dates today's chatbot invasion. The original FreeSpace 2 launched in 1999 - a more civilised age, when everybody still thought Darth Vader was an arsehole.

The Phantom Blade Zero Cui quest is one of the longest in the entire game and has some vague objectives that make it difficult to complete. Starting in the Village of Lu after finding the puppet child Cui, this quest doesn't conclude until the final region of the game. Worst of all, you can fail the quest much sooner than that if you don't have the right items or leave a specific area, blocking you out of its final reward. Having completed the quest myself, here's a full breakdown of how I found Cui's grandfather and parents in Phantom Blade.

After finding Cui in the Village of Lu smuggler's tunnel, nothing happens with this quest until you reach the Mountain of Imprisonment, which is an optional region of the game accessed via Meigu Lake – it's a crucial area for a few sidequests, including Phantom Blade Zero Whence The Weeping.To get to the mountain, you must repair the Illusory Pipa and then sail to the eastern side of the north shoreline to find the Weeping Mistgate. Once you've used the pipa to get through the mistgate, here's what you need to do:

Lu Sanqing at least has the decency to leave you a book page and the Crude Radiant Heart Accessory (though it's unfortunately not one of the best Phantom Blade Zero Accessories).

To find Cui's parents and wrap up the Cui quest, you need to get to Soulrend Cliff via Pangzhen's Mirage Estate. So, before you head there, you should finish off other objectives, such as getting inside the Phantom Blade Zero Crimson Manor and completing 'Secrets at the Heart of the Lake', which involves you fighting the Phantom Blade Zero Blizzard Blademaster. Although don't worry about the Phantom Blade Zero Triple Threat quest for now as this crops up while you're in the Mirage Estate.

This stage of the quest is much simpler than finding and helping Cui's grandfather, but bear in mind that if you have not done all the above, you will be locked out of completing these final steps:

And that's the end of the Cui quest in Phantom Blade, though it's not quite the end for Lu Jieyuan. Keep going through Soulrend Cliff and you'll soon fight the Crusher and the Saw. After beating the first phase of this boss fight, Lu Jieyuan will make a brief appearance in a cutscene. Beat the second phase and Lu Jieyuan will give you a Baishan Headband, the necessary item for Soul Tempering the Baishan Stormswords, which is one of the best dual-wield weapons in the game.

#4025. Rimworld-inspired colony sim Stardeus gets a huge update representing a year's worth of expansion and revision, with new tools for evil AI overlords

"Stardeus is in an early stage in terms of bulk and complexity, but it's already a pleasant blend of interesting ideas that generate a mostly relaxing vibe," wrote gallant star captain.exe Sin Vega in our 2022 analysis of Rimworld-influenced colony manager Stardeus. "One to watch for sure." Well, let it not be said that we weren't watching.

Stardeus has received a gargantuan early access update that has been "a year in the making," according to developer Kodo Linija. It's still a game about being an AI running a badly damaged interstellar colony ship in top-down view – sending drones to restore the damage, before waking the quarrelsome human popsicles from their slumber. But the new version introduces a quest system and a new opening tutorial chain, the ability to form alliances with other starfaring factions, the possibility of lifelong injury due to failed surgery, and the timely option to become an evil AI and mind-control your crew with beta waves, amongst other dastardly antics.

It introduces a new interface and a new ship aesthetic, a trust system that governs the odds of a mutiny, and a revised colonist skill system. There's also a freshened-up ground combat element that's now built around "cover, suppression, stuns and fleeing", and a new approach to space battles that's all about managing Flux generated when you fire weapons or take shield damage. The update notes on Steam tote more than 1,500 changes, with the dev enthusing that there is "hardly a system in the game that wasn't rebuilt, reworked or expanded".

I confess, I hadn't heard of Stardeus before. It sounds like fun, in the Dwarf Fortressian sense. The 1.0 rollout is due in "approximately Q1 2027".

#4023. Oblivion and Skyrim’s gap was bridged by forward-looking books about a murderous floating island, so why is The Elder Scrolls 6 stuck reanimating a world that’s stood still since 2011

Why the Umbri-hell has time stopped in Tamriel?

Long waits between mainline entries in a series aren’t a new phenomenon, if perhaps a bit more common nowadays due to big games' ballooning development cycles. It took about 23 years for BioWare’s Baldur's Gate 2 to be followed up by Larian’s Baldur’s Gate 3, though there were a decent amount of spin-offs and remasters peppered between the two.

The wait for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel hasn’t stretched on that long quite yet, but as Bethesda finally revealed concrete details about it just in time for Skyrim's 15th birthday, it really hit home for me that TES VI will be tasked with restoring motion to a world where calendars have been stuck in the 201st year of the 4th era since 2011. Perhaps it’s because I’m still in my twenties and haven’t lived long enough to see that many things I like pause their forward march for this long before returning. There’s also a good chance my expectations of timelines rolling forward on a regular basis without the need for a whole new entry are coloured by the constant stream of new stuff fed into most games via updates and live service passes these days.

However, when I look back at the interregnum between the last two Elder Scrolls games, Oblivion and Skyrim, I can’t help but feel that what Bethesda and ZeniMax have packed into the gap between Skyrim and Sentinel might have done the latter no favours. Sure, The Elder Scrolls Online has arguably meant that there’s been far more for series fans to sink their teeth into between mainline games than ever before, but because the MMO's a prequel, none of its tales and lore push the Elder Scrolls' timeline forwards. Meanwhile mobile and card game spin-offs like The Elder Scrolls: Blades, The Elder Scrolls: Legends, and The Elder Scrolls: Castles have all either slotted in before Skyrim or not been tied to a specific point in time.

On one hand, that leaves the devs a nice clean slate to take the sixth entry wherever they like narratively upon the conclusion of the Dragonborn’s adventures. On the other, Bethesda has missed the opportunity to paint out the world and further set up the stakes for Sentinel in the interim. Back when we were waiting for Skyrim's original release, the developers were pumping out spin-off books that daubed some fresh adventures onto the Elder Scrolls' canvas.

I bought these books - 2009’s The Infernal City and 2011’s Lord of Souls - ages ago upon hearing their tales referenced in the sorts of Elder Scrolls lore videos which appeal to sad nerds of my ilk, but have only gotten around to reading past the opening chapters in recent months.

In hindsight, I think I bounced off them that first time because it just felt a bit weird to be reading about set characters getting up to adventures in Tamriel rather than setting off on them in the boots of my own custom created protagonist. I didn’t run into the same with The Witcher, as you’re seeing that world through Gerry from the River’s eyes no matter where you turn. Anyway, the two Elder Scrolls novels by American author Greg Keyes tell the tale of the Umbriel crisis which took place 48 years after the Oblivion crisis and about 153 years before Skyrim’s dragon crisis (Tamriel does love a crisis). The Umbriel crisis saw a floating island powered by souls and formed via some Daedric drama, carve a path of destruction from Black Marsh to the Imperial City. Yep, the empire’s not-Roman soldiers had to fight a flying hunk of land. At one point some mages had to float a legion up in the sky so they could get their bottoms kicked by Umbriel’s defenders.

As you might’ve gathered, the books take the opportunity to tell a story which - especially in terms of where tech was in 2009 - wouldn’t necessarily fit an Elder Scrolls game. Or, at least, not one of the more straight-laced variety Bethesda have made in their post-Morrowind days. A lot of time’s spent looking through the eyes of two characters who’ve snuck aboard Umbriel, the floating island, after it destroyed their hometown and have to adjust to the strange customs of its inhabitant lords and their underlings before finding ways to help take it down. On the ground, things take a more familiar form, as a very serious Dark Elf named Sul and a nepo baby Imperial prince trek across bits of Cyrodiil, Morrowind, and Elsweyr on a quest to do their bit in vanquishing the threat. Then, there’s a Penitus Oculatus spy named Colin trying to figure out if the Umbriel Crisis is an inside job of some sort and a few tales of regular Imperial troops working to evacuate citizens living in the floating island’s path. In an Elder Scrolls game, you’d get some of that, but not be able to hop from person to person chapter by chapter in the fashion the books do.

Umbriel slowly floats across Black Marsh, southern Morrowind and Cyrodiil with an army of zombies in tow, much like this article’s about to float into mildly spoilery territory for the two books. You see, The Infernal City and Lord of Souls outline what happened to cause the red year, a volcanic eruption which took the land of the Dark Elves from the beautifully alien place it was at the time of The Elder Scrolls 3 and reduced it to the ash-covered wasteland it’s outlined to be at the time of Skyrim. As the latter game’s lore books would subsequently set in stone, Baar Dau - the meteor suspended in the air above Vivec City at the time of Morrowind - fell and destroyed the city following the disappearance of the metropolis’ namesake ex-Tribunal god-king. The books reveal that the big rock didn’t fall the moment Vivec vanished, but was kept afloat by a device called the Ingenium, which is essentially a magic box powered by regular soul sacrifices. Two Dunmer, Vuhon and the aforementioned Sul, ended up having a fight rooted in the tech’s murderous nature and that’s actually what led Baar Dau to finally hit the ground.

Either way, the meteor falls, but that's not an insubstantial bit of backstory for a source outside of the games to add to the Elder Scrolls’ canon. Also wound into the tale of how Umbriel came to be is a bunch of extra flesh on the bone of the relationship between Daedric prince Clavicus Vile and Umbra. In the games, the latter’s always just been a powerful sword which imprints a new personality onto its wielder, but in the books it’s portrayed as a being capable of nicking some of Vile’s godly power and plotting to escape the prince’s realm of Oblivion via the building of Umbriel. Beyond those, the books also offer a chance to get to know emperor Titus Mede I, the warlord who took over the Empire following a post-Oblivion crisis interregnum and whose offspring you murder during Skyrim’s Dark Brotherhood questline.

None of this is anything close to required knowledge for playing Skyrim. No characters from the books pop up to say hello, likely because enough time’s passed for most to perish of natural causes. The sole reference I can recall comes via a chat about a location called Sleeping Tree Camp, which isn’t tied to any of the main questlines. You can, and I did for a long time, totally ignore these time-bridging tomes. That said, I do feel that having now taken the time to read them has helped me see the history of Tamriel as something not as strictly limited to the specific snapshots in time presented by each of the games.

Tales like these, which aren’t conveyed with as much natural emotional detachment as I tend to feel when reading much-condensed accounts of historical events or far off places on the pages of in-game lore books, really help in creating the illusion that The Elder Scrolls’ world is growing and evolving as our own does. It’s not just a snow globe that only shifts whenever some prophesied hero piloted by a controller or keyboard rocks up to shake it.

I do think, in large part due to the size of the real world gap between it and Skyrim, The Elder Scrolls 6 would have and still could benefit from having spin-offs like these to keep gently nudging the timeline forwards. A complicating factor is that judging by this week’s teaser, Sentinel seems like it could be set in the 206th year of the fourth era, a mere five years after the events of Skyrim. That’d mean no 200-ish years of wiggle room in which to slot some spin-off stories without serious risk of influencing things that’d have to be reflected in the new game. Unless Bethesda wanted to either put serious barriers up around where the spin-off could tread or get into a game of arbitrarily deciding what is or isn’t canon. With some collaboration, it could certainly be done, but it could also be a headache the studio wouldn’t want.

It’s likely too late to start the ball rolling now anyway, but that doesn’t stop it being worth asking why Bethesda and their famously adaptation-loving corporate bosses at Microsoft didn’t make sure they had something akin to these books in the works when Sentinel was punted down the road in favour of Starfield.

You did this well once, why haven’t you managed to pull it off again this time? I’m hoping that isn’t the inquiry which’ll come to define The Elder Scrolls 6 as much as questions about where a chunk of the old Bethesda magic had gone did with the studio’s trip to space. Lest the next long wait for a game from them be packed with even more uncomfortable silence.

#4021. "Arkane is profitable," say Marvel's Blade developers in fiery new statement, "just not profitable enough for Microsoft"

Unionised workers reiterate call for a "solid offer" for Arkane Lyon's future

Unionised workers at Dishonored developers Arkane Lyon have published a fresh statement about the progress of negotiations with Microsoft over the studio's potential closure. Aside from calling on Xbox management to make a redundancy offer proportionate to Microsoft's colossal market value, they accuse the parent company of creating the very economic conditions cited as a reason for closing Arkane, and thereby "sabotaging" development of the forthcoming Marvel's Blade.

Published by French union Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo - one of two unions who represent workers at Arkane, the other being Printemps écologique, who didn't issue a similar message - the official English translation of the statement begins by insisting that "work on Blade is going fine". It maintains that the game will measure up to previous Arkane Lyon releases, despite the stress of trying to pin down a new owner for the company, after Microsoft announced plans to part ways with Arkane and several other studios back in July. The writers then take Microsoft to task for making an "outrageously low" redundancy offer to Arkane's workers, and further accuse the Xbox company of essentially setting Arkane up to fail by imposing a hiring freeze and depriving the studio of resources.

"Microsoft chose to justify the closure on economic reasons," the workers write. "But Microsoft is actually why those economic reasons even exist." It asserts that Microsoft froze hiring "for 19 months, which artificially caused delay and additional cost", only to then use those delays and extra costs "as a reason to close down the studio". It also claims that Microsoft have "systematically" deprived Arkane of cash, by means of corporate mechanisms the statement doesn't make wholly clear. "Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game," the statement adds, without going into detail.

"The truth is that Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic, in which our lives, projects and dreams are voided, so we can better serve Microsoft’s short term financial goals," the workers continue. They accuse Microsoft of "the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimization", citing years of mass layoffs across the Xbox company together with the recent voluntary buyout offering. "Arkane is profitable," they add. "Just not profitable enough for Microsoft."

The workers want a "solid offer" from Microsoft regarding the studio's post-Xbox future, declaring that "when the company who decided that Arkane has to shut down is, according to many sources the most profitable in the world, with a net profit of more than 133 Billions of dollars in the past years, it would be the bare minimum to ensure that the redundancy plan offered by Microsoft is on [par] with their means."

If Arkane have to close, the unionised workers call on Microsoft "to release funds commensurate with Microsoft’s status as a corporation, to make sure that the workers are compensated in line with the loss suffered". They'd like a redundancy payment of €200,000, two years of "redeployment support", a package of "shared resources for training and studio creation", including a residual bonus, and "compensation up to the redundancy payment for independent workers’ contract breach", to safeguard the livelihoods of freelancers and contractors.

The warring parties at Xbox and Arkane have until 11th December this year to figure out a deal. Reportedly, Ubisoft are among those looking to buy Arkane - a source of some concern, given that Ubisoft have also recently closed a number of studios and laid many people off. I'm not sure I'd be waving my wallet around if I were using my other hand to sign pink slips.

#4020. "BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy" argues petition calling on Canadian government to step in

1,662 Canadians have been verified as signing it thus far

Calls for the Canadian government to help ressurect recently shuttered RPG makers BioWare have progressed from a single post by a politician to a petition with enough signatures that it looks set to be presented to the Canadian House of Commons for an official response. So far, 1,662 people from the country of maple syrup and also other things have signed this call for their leaders to consider stepping in.

"BioWare is one of Canada's most important cultural exports to the world in the 21st century, selling tens of millions of units of their video games globally," declares the petition, started by Brendan Routh and authorised by Vancouver Kingsway MP Don Davies.

"BioWare's productions champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights that are at the centre of Canada's national identity," its run of bullet points continues. "BioWare has been shuttered by its American parent company Electronic Arts, now owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners and BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy."

With all of that in mind, the petition calls on the Canadian Government to "provide BioWare with the capital necessary to secure independence of themselves and their intellectual property from Electronic Arts and resume business as an independent, Canadian company". The Canadians who've signed also want their leaders to "protect Canadian businesses and cultural institutions from being dictated by American and foreign corporate interests" and "champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights at the centre of Canada's national identity by preserving BioWare's invaluable contribution to the global entertainment industry".

Thus far, the petition's amassed 1,662 verified signatures from citizens across Canada, putting it above the 500 verified signature threshold required for it to be presented to the country's House of Commons. That'll be followed by the tabling of an official response from the Canadian government.

As with some of the responses from political bodies the likes of the Stop Killing Games campaign have gotten over the years, I find it hard not to see this petition not being greeted with an answer along the lines of 'We do care about this and thank you for raising it, but we're not really gonna do much here'. I think a full BioWare resurrection with government backing is highly unlikely, but finding some way to enshrine the studio's legacy or contribution to Canada's games industry and arts culture seems a lot more easily doable.

A big statue of Blokeshep and Femshep surrounded by their crew of potential allies somewhere in Edmonton, maybe. Or a big stone middle finger that's always required to be aimed at a poster for the next Star Wars film/game/TV show/bit of merch.

There's a golden rule of storage: no matter how much you have, it's never quite enough. Nevertheless, Kioxia is taking that principle to its limits, as it's announced "a new storage density milestone" in the form of 640 of its 245.76 TB enterprise SSDs chained together to create just over 157 petabytes worth of storage in a single rack cabinet.

157 petabytes is... well, it's 157 million gigabytes. Enough storage space for God of War: Ragnarok, a 190 GB game, to be installed over 820,000 times.

And yes, it's been designed for AI data centers. The "storage solution" (I do hate that term) has been created in collaboration with Dell, and essentially amounts to 16 PowerEdge R7725xd servers, each stuffed with 40 Kioxia LC9 Series drives inside one industry-standard 42U server rack.

"As AI workloads drive continued growth in unstructured data, organizations need storage that can deliver higher capacity without a corresponding increase in data center floor/rack space, power consumption or cooling requirements," says the press gumph. "High-capacity NVMe SSDs can help address these demands by consolidating more data into a smaller, more efficient infrastructure footprint."

Which seems timely. With physical data center size becoming an increasing issue (not least because massive data center buildouts are a tad unpopular right now), cramming as much storage as possible into a single rack is sure to save on some concrete, at the very least.

But I'm not going to suggest this sort of excessive consumption is anything but jarring, given us little ol' consumers are counting our pennies in the middle of a NAND flash crisis. Have you seen the price of game-ready SSDs recently? I have. It ain't pretty.

But hey, at least we know where 157 petabytes-worth of raw flash capacity is going. Straight into one of these rack cabinets, where it can be used for all sorts of AI-related purposes. The sometimes-intelligent beast needs feeding, and Kioxia and Dell appear to have worked very hard to fit its lunch inside one handy box.

#4018. You can now play Pillars of Eternity and Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire with a controller on PC from start to finish, thanks to a new update open for testing

Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also gotten a makeover

After gifting Pillars of Eternity a turn-based mode for its tenth anniversary, Obsidian have now rolled out full PC controller support for both the RPG and its younger sibling Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire. The support, along with some tweaks to Deadfire's turn-based mode, are currently out in public test form.

"You can now play the whole of either game with a controller, from character creation to the end credits (and, in Deadfire, all the way out to naval combat), in both real-time with pause and turn-based mode," the studio wrote in their announcement of the public test going live. "Deadfire’s support builds on the controller scheme from the console editions. Prefer to switch things up? Pick up your mouse and keyboard at any time, and the game follows right along."

"Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also been reworked with the improvements we made for Pillars of Eternity’s turn-based mode: turns now follow each character’s speed, combat is more lethal, and swapping weapons or drinking potions no longer costs your action. You can now switch turn-based mode on or off during a playthrough, and the update brings a long list of fixes across combat, quests, audio, and the interface."

Both Xbox and PlayStation controllers are included in the support, along with the Steam Deck and Steam's Big Picture mode. Radial menus have been worked in to allow rapid firing of abilities, spells, and party commands, with the interface also popping up the right button prompts for your controller of choice.

These additions are all part of Patch 1.3.10.0, the full notes for which can be found in the post I've embedded above, alongside instructions on how to get into the public test. The patch also does things like ensure "the description of Fulvano’s Boots is no longer fragmented". I'm glad Obsidian have saved those soles.

The studio haven't put a concrete end date on the test at this point, instead noting it "will run for some time as we continue to update it in preparation for a full release". As it's a test, those jumping in should expect bugs and other funkiness.

#4017. Microsoft Thinks Xbox 'Pioneered' Dual Analogue Controllers

It’s a big month for Xbox as it celebrates its 25th anniversary, with lots of entertaining initiatives underway – including a pretty cool website where it tracks your entire history with the brand.

But in a big – and otherwise interesting – celebratory blog post, boss Asha Sharma appears to have mixed up some of the facts.

Writing about the original Xbox, which launched 15th November 2001, she claims the console “pioneered dual analogue controllers”.

It’s obviously not a big deal, but this is blatantly not true.

While the Xbox innovated in a number ways – namely including a hard drive and ethernet port, which paved the way for the industry changing Xbox Live – dual analogue controllers had already been introduced four years earlier with the PS1.

While it’s true the DualShock wasn’t originally included with Sony’s console as standard, that changed with the PS2’s release in 2000, over a year before the original Xbox arrived.

I wondered whether Sharma may have meant to write “dual analogue triggers” here, but that’s also not true; the Dreamcast’s controller, for example, introduced pressure-sensitive triggers as early as 1999.

So, I’m not exactly sure what Microsoft thinks it invented here, but it sure wasn’t dual analogue controllers!

Hence Sony "tacked on" the Left-Stick in the secondary position and retained the D-Pad in the optimum ergonomic position for primary directional control, just as it was located on the original digital PS1 controller.

Everyone else (Nintendo/Microsoft) later swapped the D-Pad to the secondary position and the directional analogue stick to the primary position when it became clear that analogue control was now the majority control method for almost all games.

#4016. Goddess of Victory: Nikke's PC launcher suffers potential malware infection, with its publishers suggesting folks who've booted since late September do a security check

A cruel twist for the Shift Up-developed epic shooter RPG of cruel humanity destiny

Goddess of Victory: Nikke, a gacha shooter/RPG developed by Stellar Blade makers Shift Up, has suffered a "security incident" which has seen its PC launcher potentially be infected with third-party malware. Thankfully, it seems a patch to make the launcher safe again has been quickly dished out, but publishers Level Infinite are still advising players who've booted the game up since September 27th to do some security checks.

"We have identified that some files in the NIKKE Windows PC launcher were recently tampered with by a third party, potentially allowing malicious programs to run when the launcher was launched," the developers of the game with anime girls who - judging by the promo art - breast boobily announced yesterday. "As a result, your PCs and account information may have been exposed to security risks.

"We are continuing to investigate the extent of the potential damage and review appropriate response measures. We are also conducting a thorough review of our network security environment, including our CDN, to determine how the PC launcher files were compromised. We will take all necessary precautions to prevent further damage and ensure that this issue does not happen again. We deeply regret that this security incident has caused Commanders significant concern and distress, when our responsibility should have been to provide a safe gaming environment."

In order to try and help players "scan for and remove the malicious programs distributed in this incident", publishers Level Infinite have added a feature to Nikke's official PC client that does just that. They're advising that anyone who's booted up the game at least once after September 27th at 15:41 (UTC+9) use that or perform a manual security check.

Once that's done, affected players are advised to change the passwords for any accounts they've used on the PC they used to boot the launcher, as well as generate new API keys and access tokens. "We take very seriously the possibility that this incident may have affected not only your gaming experience but also your PC, accounts with external services, and personal assets," Level Infinite added. "If you believe you may have been affected by this issue or suffered from any loss, please contact our customer support team. We will review each inquiry carefully and respond as promptly as possible."

Going forwards, they plan to improve their monitoring "so that any unauthorized file modifications or security threats can be detected early and addressed promptly", as well as "establish an integrity verification system for external resources accessed by the PC launcher" and ensure the launcher only requires "the minimum permissions necessary".

Here's hoping the studio are able to keep things more secure in the future and that affected players are able to get rid of any malware with minimal suffering or inconvenience.

This might be the best chassis of 2026. It doesn't tick all the boxes perfectly, but what it does do at this price is deliver an exceptionally good looking case, with plenty of cable management, and a primo build experience that puts even some of the bigger case manufacturers to shame. Available in both black and white, for those looking for a modest rig that'll look good on your desk, the C6 Curve is it.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

Shangri-la, the promised land. Aside from the very notion of that concept being oh so appetising in the chaotic world that is 2026, there's something of that in the C6 Curve Air. An odd way to start a chassis review, I'll admit, particularly one that genuinely, I think is probably one of the best PC cases of 2026, but it's more than a metaphor here.

This feels like something a little special this case. It feels like how Corsair's 4000D series felt, or NZXT's H7 lineup when that first debuted, or even Phanteks' Evolv arsenal from way back when at the start of my tech journalism career. There's something iconic here, that I can't quite place my finger on, something that I think is massively underrated in the world of custom rigs. Refined subtlety.

Honestly the C6 Curve Air feels as if it's some bastard love child of the Phanteks Evolv series, Asus's Pro Art line and Fractal Design's North variants. Born in secret, and somehow less than $100.

It's clean, modest, with an elegant aesthetic, good choice of materials, dependable internal layout, decent cable management, and it's genuinely a chassis that I can't stop looking at. It's not flawless, nothing ever is, but what Antec has done here is, particularly in a market that's so over saturated with tempered glass black obelisks, is impressive.

✅ You want a budget, clean chassis that stands out from the crowd: With curved tempered glass, a stylish base, and a remarkably crisp interior at an outstanding price point the C6 Curve Air, is one of the best looking affordable cases you can find on the market today.

✅ You're using a massive graphics card: Bells and whistles are minimal in the C6 Curve Air to save on cost of manufacturing, which means there's no anti-sag bracket included. If you're using a larger triple-slot, pick up an aftermarket anti-sag mount elsewhere.

1x USB 3.2 Type-C, 2x USB 3.2 Type-A, 3.5 mm headphone jack

2x 120 mm PSU SHROUD; 3x 120 mm/2x140 mm ROOF; 1x 120/140 mm REAR

ATX (160 mm side-mounted, 150mm traditional)

At a surface level, there's not a huge amount to talk about here in terms of overall featureset. It's a typical mid-tower case, it's got support for ATX, there's some nice rubber grommets built in to hide the cables protruding from the rear, it's got a full PSU shroud, and some fairly modest fan and rad mounting locations dotted around the place, and well that's about it. The big standout feature is of course, the tempered glass. It's curved along the front edges, and wraps around midway back through the rear of the chassis, but there's no special innovative, screaming from the rooftops technical element at play here.

That glass is a curious decision as well, because it cuts your case cable management space down in half, and there's no additional intake mounting points either, nor front nor side, other than the two (included) 120 mm fans situated in the floor itself.

But here's the thing with the C6 Curve Air. These small seemingly mundane features that it has, that we've seen in cases for the last ten years, are so well refined, that it's almost like a complete fresh launch.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

Take the intake fans. They're twin 120 mm reverse blade designs, recessed into the floor of the PSU shroud. Now, that's a space usually taken up by a hard drive caddy (which very few of us use), and an abundance of excess stuffed cables. To counter that, Antec's opted for no caddy there at all, leaving one mounting location on the back of the CPU tray, and redesigned the entire PSU area, so it's rotational by its nature.

You can slot a 160 mm PSU in here, sideways, with a power lead passthrough, and route all the cables directly up the back of the motherboard tray. No need for a Corsair RMx Shift here, no sir, any old PSU will do. That means, cable management routes are remarkably direct, and there's little mess to manage or tight corners to wrap your cables around.

As for the actual cable management, there's not a mad amount of support here either. There's a few velcro straps, and three plastic clips on the right, and those rubber grommets and that's it, but it's enough, and if you tuck your extra SATA cables out of the way, those twin 120 mm intakes have plenty of space to pull air up and through. It's actually one of the cleanest cable managed cases I've built, and there's not a single tie in sight.

Both sides, and the entire base of the chassis are well ventilated as well, with either that pristine slat design lining the front and edges, or pure perforations, so cool airflow is ample. It's all just very well thought out.

The only thing that mildly irked me, was a lack of a removable radiator bracket, (which would've made subsequent cable management at the end considerably easier), and there's no GPU anti-sag bracket either, which has almost become a staple in modern designs.

And that's all coming in at just around the $100 mark, if not cheaper. Antec, also has a white variant available too, for a little extra if you do fancy something a bit punchier in terms of the overall aesthetic.

There are alternatives out there, that allow you to fit more kit in, mount more fans etc, but few cases feel quite as good as what you're getting here. Hyte's Y40 is a good example, or Lian Li's O11 Vision Compact.

And of course you can get some flashier cases as well, Phanteks' XT View Matrix with its full dot grid display, again fits in that groove. But none of them feel particularly timeless compared to this.

There is one caveat to all of this of course, and that's long term future viability here. Although the case design itself will last for many years to come, let's say hypothetically RAM and silicon manufacturing ramp up by 300% in the next two years somehow, and datacenter demand drops (we can only hope), and you do want to build a new machine with new more power hungry hardware, I do have some concern that those twin 120 mm intakes, might not be quite enough to cool both a thirsty GPU and CPU combo longer into the future.

I've waxed lyrically about how this thing looks visually already, but it's worth stressing because it's a thing of beauty. There is absolutely something "ProArty" about the C6 Curve Air. Even if it's just its design philosophy. The slats, the power button, the understated lack of lighting, the curved glass. It's undeniably luscious in scope. Heck even that roof panel, slimline, compact, smooth against the top just sings to the overall design, and that blend of perforated mesh around the PSU area, sits strikingly against the slats feeding the intake fans, and it really stands out.

It's overall a little wider than you'd think for a mid-tower, particularly given the height (in part to accommodate the rotated PSU), but given we've got so many cuboid styled dual chamber cases these days, I'm not opposed to a little extra girth (don't quote me on that).

Perhaps, and this is very debatable, but perhaps it's just slightly too understated? A touch of integrated LED lighting, just a soft warm white glow somewhere, shining up inside the interior, and illuminating your hardware, following the old adage, show the light, not the lightbulb, would work a treat in this thing. It's the first aftermarket addition I'd look at adding that's for sure, as it'd just give it a bit more depth inside.

As for building in the C6 Curve Air, it's a fairly smooth ride. The first major hurdle I came across was actually dismantling the chassis. I tend not to look at instruction manuals on a new case, because in my mind, it should be intuitive. There's only so many ways you can attach things to a black box afterall.

The glass side panel pops off and out from the rear, and then slides up. The rear metal panel does the same, as does the secondary rear glass panel too. You pull up from the rear of the roof panel to grab the underside there, and then you're left with that front curved glass, and the two PSU shroud covers. For the PSU covers, simply pull them up from the bottom, and as for the front, I for the life of me couldn't figure out how to remove it. You can remove two philips screws, and then tilt it out away from the main spine, but it doesn't seem to come up and out like the others, at least not easily. That is fine really, as you can leave that on anyway. There's no fans to mount here, and it acts as a brace for the whole structure.

Other things to note, there is of course that passthrough PSU plate on the back. You can remove that if you're running a short 150 mm PSU, but if you're using a 160 mm you'll need to rotate the unit, and then hook it up to the passthrough. Antec's included a cutout to thread the passthrough cable through as well, although it will depend on the positioning of the port on your power supply. Remember to keep the PSU with the fan facing down, as the shroud is solid above it.

Cable management on the whole was surprisingly impressive. There's not a ton that you can do here. Antec has included two velcro straps to help manage the 24-pin and front I/O cables, and then there's some plastic clips on the right (designed for fans, but I stuck EPS power in here as well), and that's it, but surprisingly, combined with the rubber grommets, it was enough. I used a total of one cable tie in this entire build, and to be fair, I'd already pre-strapped that to the 12VHPWR cable anyway prior to this system.

The only downsides during my time with the C6 Curve Air came in the form of the lack of a radiator bracket, (which meant I ended up fiddling for far too long trying to plug in the pump), and there's no GPU anti sag solution anywhere. Although to be fair, I'm not exactly sure where you'd fit one in this design.

So, it's a good case, we've established that, but is there anything we can do during the build process to make it better? Well if it was my own rig, I'd be looking at shifting the fan layout, away from a traditional setup. Keep the two 120 mm floor intakes as is (maybe shift them out to something with a bit more pushing power), but then I'd also swap the 360 mm AIO exhausts to act as intakes instead. A ballsy move, working against thermodynamics, I get it, but I'd absolutely test whether overall you'd see better temps long-term with that config. That way you've got a five in, one out solution, for massive positive pressure, in exchange for slightly higher CPU temps.

On the cable management front, keep your cabling as minimal as possible, remove any you don't need, but even if you leave them in, it's not the end of the world, and lastly I'd leave installing the radiator, until the very end (before the GPU), once all the cables had been plugged in (including the pump and CPU fans), just to make life a little easier.

Oh and 100% install the PSU rotated, rather than removing that rear bracket. It just gives you so much more space, and I can't stress enough, just how easy it is routing those cable runs as a result.

4. Best budget compact: Thermaltake S100 TG Snow Edition

This might be the best chassis of 2026. It doesn't tick all the boxes perfectly, but what it does do at this price is deliver an exceptionally good looking case, with plenty of cable management, and a primo build experience that puts even some of the bigger case manufacturers to shame. Available in both black and white, for those looking for a modest rig that'll look good on your desk, the C6 Curve is it.

#4014. Nvidia ensure unboxing a ludicrously expensive new graphics card isn't limited to real life in these RAM crisis times by releasing a GeForce 8800 GTX unpacking sim

Hey at least the card in this bit of 2006 nostalgia bait has only cost you a virtual arm and leg

In what feels a fairly cheeky move during a time when memory shortages have infamously made it pretty much impossible to buy a decently powerful new graphics card without spending approximately a gazillion pounds/dollars/dollarpounds, Nvidia have decided to put out a Steam demo that allows folks to re-live the feeling of unboxing a ludicrously expensive graphics card in 2006.

The demo, dubbed GeForce 8800 GTX - 20 Years of a Legend, has been developed by Dylan Browne. He previously made Through The Ages, a "real-time high end graphical cinematic that takes us on a nostalgic journey through three of NVIDIA's iconic GPUs" which is also on Steam for reasons.

The GeForce 8800 GTX demo, as you might've guessed, is a tribute to that specific card in the form of a tech demo simulating what it was like to unbox one in a mid-2000s bedroom. Seriously, there's a copy of Crysis on the desk so you know this is the domain of a true devotee to the best graphics available in around 2007.

"Step into a 2006-era PC gaming room, unbox the GeForce 8800 GTX, inspect it up close, and install it in an era-accurate PC tower," the demo's description declares. "Explore nods to GeForce history and hidden easter eggs as DLSS 4.5 with Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, Ray Reconstruction, path tracing, and Mega Geometry bring the nostalgic setting to life. From holding the card to the glow of the monitor, rediscover a moment in PC gaming history - or experience it for the first time!"

As the GeForce 8800 GTX was a top-line card that cost $599 on release in 2006 - about $1,000 in today's money if the online inflation calculator I've just used is on the money - this isn't really a 'we know cards are ludicrously expensive right now, but here's a reminder of when you used to be able to actually afford to unbox one' sort of demo. It is at least a free way to virtually experience having blown a chunk of your savings on something that can render really sexy textures without the existential dread of doing so in real life.

Well, I say that, I've just noticed the minimum requirements for the demo note that you'll need an RTX 4070 card. So, depending on your current setup, this might well be a case of Nvidia offering the chance to render unboxing a card you couldn't afford in 2006 via a card you can't afford in 2026.

Is that about the best we can all hope for in 2026? Probably.

#4013. Apex Legends adds a grumpy, teamwiping Godzilla to its growing history of unappealing crossovers

No doubt eager as peas to help pay off EA's billions in debt, battle royale shooter Apex Legends is set to run another of its intellectual propertytastic crossover events. This one, starting on November 10th, stars Godzilla, of Godzilla Minus Zero, Godzilla vs. Kong, Godzilla (1954), Godzilla 2000: Millennium, Godzilla (1998), Son of Godzilla, and Godzilla (2014). I might be missing some.

Besides a profitable range of weapon and character skins, most of which appear to have hot glue gunned an 70-year film franchise's worth of dorsal fins all over themselves, the King of the Monsters himself will show up on the game's Storm Point map. He does at least have more than a background cameo: he'll occasionally blast an area with Legend-melting atomic breath, though brave souls who risk the danger zone can score a custom Devotion LMG with a unique heat ray attack of its own.

Worth noting also that the character skins are each based on a certain 'zilla movie, though as our freelance news writer and associate Large Lizard Cinema expert Ashley isn't working today, I'm not sure which of these are from hits and which are the duds. Walking wallhack motherfucker Bloodhound gets the newest fashion, their skin being inspired by Minus Zero, while my personal favourite Scottish scientist Horizon gets duds based on Big G in Godzilla vs. Destoroyah. Octane's skin is taken from... something called a Jet Jaguar? Google suggests this may in fact be elite Godzilla knowledge, something I clearly lack.

Regardless, and with the understanding that a lot of effort goes into these crossovers, I still kinda wish they didn't exist? Even putting aside basic game-playing problems with how, for example, wacky skins interfere with Legend silhouettes – you couldn't pay me to initiate a fight against a full team of near-identical Gundampeople - it's just icky to have an otherwise sharp, smart, at times fiercely competitive battle royale turned into an animated billboard for a few days.

Besides, Apex already has its own kaiju: the sleepy, pacifist Leviathans that innocently wandered into the King's Canyon map for a few of the earlier seasons. I consider these much better Friend Material than Godzilla, on the grounds that they'd only kill you by accident, and it was usually your own fault - by wandering under their briefly raised megahooves - anyway.

A "server issue" knocked both games offline, across all platforms, for nearly two weeks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A little less than two weeks after their multiplayer features were taken offline because of a mysterious "server issue," multiplayer functionality in Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3 has been restored, meaning invasions and messages are once again working as they should.

Word of the service restoration game via a very businesslike message on the Dark Souls website: "Regarding the temporary suspension of the game server for Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3, the investigation has been completed and the fix has been applied. The game server and online features are now restored.

"We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience caused, and thank you for your patience and understanding."

So what exactly went wrong? Well, that's the mysterious part. Aside from intermittent apologies for the inconvenience and thanks for your patience in messages posted to X, FromSoft's had nothing to say about it—and that remains the case now: It's back, be happy, speak of the matter no more.

Whatever happened, it clearly wasn't as serious a problem as the 2022 mess that saw PC servers for all Dark Souls games shut down for the better part of a year. In that case, FromSoft copped to the problem: A security vulnerability that allowed malicious code to be executed via the games' online services. But that fix was also long in coming because FromSoft was busy with other things, like finishing Elden Ring, which was kind of a big deal.

Anyway, aside from the relative brevity of the downtime, we had something else that made the outage a little more bearable than it was back in '22: The Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3 Seamless Co-op mods that operate independently of FromSoft's servers. They also enable a far more flexible multiplayer experience than what's offered by the games themselves, letting players team up to run through the games at will, and without having to deal with disconnects when somebody dies or a boss gets smoked.

But if your preference is for the chaos of native Dark Souls multiplayer? Now that option's back on the table too.

#4011. Was This New Fable Gameplay Meant to Sell the Game?

I am pretty confident Fable will be a fantastic RPG when it finally releases in February 2027, but for those still sat on the fence, Xbox is going to have to do a better job of promoting it than this latest example.

To mark the 25th anniversary of Xbox, four minutes of gameplay taken from a quest has been uploaded. However, all of maybe 30 seconds of it actually has anything going on. Watch it above.

Obviously, you do indeed do a lot of walking during open world RPGs, but it's not something you usually feature much in marketing beats. That's what most of the latest gameplay slice for Fable is, though: walking.

Partway through, there is a combat sequence showing off swordfighting, archery, and magical abilities. It's over quickly, however, and then we're back to walking. The video then concludes with a cutscene lacking context as it's been plucked out of the full game to be seen online.

I grew up playing the three mainline Fable games on the Original Xbox and Xbox 360; I have very fond memories of this series, so I want the new rebooted instalment to do well. It'll need better presentations and trailers than this for a good chance at that. It's out for PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC on 23rd February 2027.

What do you make of the video? Share your thoughts in the comments below.

An entire battalion's worth of new Lego Star Wars sets have dropped out of hyperspace like a Rebel fleet about to take on the Empire, and while they look incredible (I'm genuinely excited to grab some of these), I'm most interested in the bizarro minifigures some come with.

Unveiled at the Lego store as part of A New Hope's 50th anniversary, there are seven new Lego Star Wars sets in total spanning a host of budgets and styles. The lineup includes massive display pieces you can hang on your wall alongside dioramas and playsets, but a few have a special bonus feature - an extra minifigure based on concept art for the original Star Wars. Han Solo, Luke Skywalker, Darth Vader, and Princess Leia all looked pretty different with their original designs, and they stand out from their usual iterations from the best Lego sets. You can see them in the image above.

Want a better look at the sets themselves? I've listed them below, and they all hit shelves at the beginning of January 2027.

Made up of 718 pieces, this Empire Strikes Back diorama recreates one of the most famous moments (and lines) in movie history. It's quite a lot bigger than the 295-piece version we got 10 years ago. This one also features an extra concept art minifigure version of Darth Vader.UK: £69.99 at Lego

This is one of the cheaper 50th Anniversary sets so far, and the smallest; it's 372 pieces. However, it comes on a diorama base with two minifigures (Obi-Wan and Anakin), so should serve well as either a display piece or a playset for younger Padawans who want to recreate that pivotal moment from Revenge of the Sith. It also comes with a concept art version of Han Solo, back when he had a lightsaber in early drafts.UK: £34.99 at Lego

I think this might be one of the nicest minifigure-scale ships Lego's put out in quite a while, with exposed studs and greebles brilliantly recreating the Y-Wing's scrappy design. It comes with a concept art version of Luke Skywalker, who is markedly different from the final design; he's rocking a gas mask and has a yellow lightsaber in tow.UK: £69.99 at Lego

At 23 inches (59cm) tall and with 3,209 pieces behind it, this display piece is gonna take pride of place in any collection. It cleverly recreates the original 1970s New Hope poster in 3D, and it's stunning. While most have to wait until January 4, members of the free Lego Insiders program get early access from January 1.UK: £269.99 at Lego

I was a little confused when I first saw this kit, because it wasn't clear what else it could become... but the answer is very cool and quite unexpected. Besides being an imposing rendition of Darth's helmet, it can also be made into Vader's lit lightsaber behind the words "I am your father." Either way, the box contains 628 pieces.UK: £59.99 at Lego

Did you know that Stormtroopers almost looked like this? The fearsome design featured in concept art for A New Hope, and now you can immortalize it on your shelf. Sadly, this one doesn't come with any extras.UK: £69.99 at Lego

Creating huge versions of minifigures has really taken off for Lego recently, and we got a Darth Vader version a little while back... so it's only right that the hero of the story gets their own. It's made up of 981 pieces, and comes with a concept art version of Princess Leia.UK: £89.99 at Lego

Speaking of new kits, a Lego Yoshi set has been teased for 2027, and clues suggest it'll be pretty big.
